title: Canary deploy surge -> scheduler saturation postmortem
content:
Summary:

On 2024-10-31 18:12 UTC we observed an increase in pod start latencies and a spike in evictions in the us-west gpu nodepool. The root cause was a misconfigured canary rollout for the new autoscaler patch (deploy/canary-autoscaler) which caused ~20k short-lived pods to be scheduled in a 6 minute window. The scheduler CPU usage and scheduling queue depth spiked, causing broad start delays and eventual eviction waves on memory-constrained nodes. Impact: customer-facing inference queues experienced tokenization latency increases (~3–8x p95) and several dedicated jobs timed out. No data loss; primary impact was increased tail latency and a set of customer jobs retried.

Key metrics observed (approx):
- Scheduling queue depth: baseline ~50 -> peak ~7,200
- kube-scheduler CPU: baseline 120m -> peak 1,900m (sustained for 4m)
- Pod start p95: baseline 2s -> peak 45s (for pods targeted at the gpu pool)
- Evictions (OOM) in gpu pool: 0 -> 34 within incident window
- Customer API p95 token latency: baseline 130ms -> incident peak 1.1s

Timeline (UTC):
- 18:10: deploy/canary-autoscaler rollout initiated (automated canary job)
- 18:12: pager alerts: scheduler high cpu, pod-start p95 > 10s
- 18:13–18:18: burst of small-lived pods (cron-triggered jobs with low request limits) created by canary job; k8s events show rapid creation -> pending states
- 18:14: SREs escalated; initial mitigation attempted: increased scheduler replicas (no effect)
- 18:16: first eviction wave observed on several gpu nodes; node pressure alarms triggered
- 18:18: scaled down canary by aborting rollout (manual rollback of canary job)
- 18:21: creation rate subsided; scheduler queue gradually drained over next 8–12 minutes
- 18:40: all affected pods either started or rescheduled; alerts gradually resolved

Detection and monitoring notes:
- Primary signal came from scheduler CPU and custom pod-start-duration monitors.
- There was no single application metric that triggered first; it was the aggregated SLO alert (pod start p95) followed by scheduler telemetry.
- The canary job itself emitted normal metrics; it did not exceed per-pod quotas but the aggregate burst exceeded assumptions.

What happened (analysis):
1) Canary orchestration logic in deploy/canary-autoscaler used a fanout pattern to validate autoscaler behavior by creating small test jobs across all nodepools. A recent change removed a randomized jitter and increased job concurrency from 5 -> 50 (intended to speed up validation).
2) The canary controller runs from a central CI namespace and wasn’t rate-limited by the cluster API. The burst of ~20k pods was within quota per-namespace but not within cluster scheduling capacity expectations.
3) Scheduler has an observed weakness with deep queue backpressure: when queue depth jumps above ~2k items, scheduling throughput drops nonlinearly due to internal contention in predicate/prioritizer cycles, amplified by expensive node resource checks (GPU/accelerator predicates) and taint/toleration calculations.
4) The GPU nodepool had many pods with tight memory limits and a few heavy resident system pods; when the scheduler attempted to place many small pods, some nodes' available memory dipped and Kubelet evicted lower-priority pods (OOM), which in turn increased reschedules and made the scheduling pressure worse (positive feedback loop).

Commands / evidence snippets (sanitized):
- kubectl get deployments deploy/canary-autoscaler -n ci-canary -o yaml (showing concurrency change)
- k8s event sample during burst:
  2024-10-31T18:13:21Z  Normal  Created    pod/test-canary-8t7k   Created container
  2024-10-31T18:13:21Z  Warning Pending     pod/test-canary-8t7k   scheduling attempts: insufficient resources
- scheduler metrics (prometheus): scheduler_queue_depth{…}=7200 at 18:14:03 UTC
- kube-scheduler_cpu_seconds_total jump from 120m -> 1.9 CPU (graph attached in the linked ticket)

Immediate mitigations (what we did):
- 18:16: aborted the canary run and scaled down canary-controller concurrency (manual stop).
- 18:17: temporarily cordoned a subset (3) of most-constrained gpu nodes to prevent further eviction cascades while we drained the scheduling queue.
- 18:20: applied a temporary admission controller rate-limit using a webhook that enforces creation QPS for the ci-canary namespace (quick patch).
- 18:25: added temporary horizontal autoscaler to scheduler to increase replicas from 1 -> 3, which helped but did not fully restore throughput until the creation rate subsided.

Root causes (summary):
- Primary: Canary orchestration removed safety jitters and increased concurrency, producing an aggregate burst that exceeded scheduling throughput assumptions.
- Secondary: Scheduler throughput nonlinearity under deep queue load (depends on predicate complexity for GPU nodes) and lack of cluster-level creation-rate throttling for CI/canary namespaces.
- Tertiary: GPU node memory headroom was lower than expected due to resident system pods; eviction thresholds were aggressive and allowed an eviction cascade once scheduling latency lengthened.

Contributing factors:
- Canary run had no cluster-wide creation-rate budget enforced (namespace-only quotas existed but were permissive).
- No preflight simulation for aggregate object creation used by the canary workflow.
- Scheduler profiling for deep-queue behavior had not been run in Q3; our internal docs warned of degradation but it was deprioritized.

Follow-ups / action items (owners and ETA):
- Add a low-latency creation-rate guard for CI/canary namespaces via OPA/Gatekeeper (owner: Riley ; ETA: 2024-11-20).
- Reintroduce randomized jitter and cap concurrency in canary controller; add automated preflight that simulates cluster-wide QPS (owner: Diego ; ETA: 2024-11-08) – PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/k8s-ops/pull/987
- Scheduler: run dedicated profiling for queue depth > 2k and file priority optimizations (owner: Tom ; ETA: 2024-12-01).
- GPU nodepool: increase memory headroom by 5% and reduce eviction aggressiveness (owner: Priya ; ETA: 2024-11-12).
- Run an intentional failure drill to validate admission-limiter and scheduler autoscaling under a controlled burst (owner: eng-sre; ETA: 2024-11-30).
- Update on-call runbook: include explicit steps to cordon+drain policy for memory-starved accelerator pools and a checklist to abort canaries early (owner: Samira ; ETA: 2024-11-06).

Lessons learned (short):
- Small configuration changes in test/canary automation can have outsized cluster effects — treat canary controllers as first-class cluster citizens with strict rate limits.
- Scheduler behaves nonlinearly under deep-queue conditions; we need both software mitigations and operational guard rails.

Appendix / notes to reviewers:
- See incident Jira JIRA-INC-4392 for raw graphs and timeline zooms.
- Linked PR contains the reverting patch for the canary controller and the new concurrency cap.
- Slack thread includes the real-time decision log and snippets of kubectl output captured during the incident.

Notes-to-self (quick):
- Follow up with infra team about potential kernel param that exacerbates scheduling latency on nodes with many small containers.
- Consider adding a 'cluster-burst-sim' test to our CI that runs in a sandbox k8s to measure scheduling queue scaling curves (cheap version using k3s).

-- End of postmortem (drafted by Samira Patel; reviewed by Tom, Riley, Priya)
